samples.question: The picture contains one dark blue wire: a single unbranched stroke of constant thickness that wanders inside one boxed area of the picture. The wire never branches, never crosses itself and never touches itself; parallel folds of the wire are always separated by clear background. Two square stiles, each a black frame around a white core, are clamped onto the wire. Every stile is wider than the wire, so it covers the wire completely and cuts the ink into exactly three arcs: the arc that runs between the two stiles, and the two outer arcs that run from a stile to a free end of the wire. Eight small orange beads are printed on the wire. Every bead is narrower than the wire, so a bead never cuts it; beads never touch a stile and never touch each other. A bead counts as lying between the stiles only if it sits on the arc you travel when you walk along the wire's own ink from one stile to the other; stepping across background, or onto a neighbouring fold, is never a legal step. The straight line between the two stiles is not a guide: because the wire folds, beads that look enclosed between the stiles can sit on an outer arc, and beads far away from that line can sit between them. The total number of beads is always eight, so counting all the beads never gives the answer. All gray shapes anywhere in the picture are decoration and mean nothing. How many orange beads lie on the arc of wire between the two stiles? Answer 2, 3, 4 or 5.
